    Industry observers note that the American Express® Gold Card is one of the best cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and it also has an excellent welcome offer. The card is ideal for anyone who spends a lot on dining, whether at restaurants or supermarkets, and in my experience, getting approved for the card is quite easy.

    The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), though the card also offers up to $424 in annual credits, which could more than offset the annual fee, not even accounting for all the other perks.

    Now, a vast majority of cardmembers aren’t going to maximize all the Amex Gold Card credits, since it is a bit of a “coupon book” vibe, in terms of how the credits are issued. In this post, I’d like to take a look at the Amex Gold Card credits, including the restrictions, and how they can be redeemed.

    Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card.

    With the Amex Gold Card credits, cardmembers can potentially receive statement credits with Uber, select dining establishments, Resy, and Dunkin’. The terms associated with using each of these Amex Gold credits varies, so it’s worth covering all the details. Below is a chart with the basics, and then I’ll cover all the credits in more detail. (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

    The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:.

    According to recent reports, what’s my take on the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit? As someone who uses both Uber and Uber Eats more than once per month, the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit benefit is basically as good as cash to me. Obviously if you don’t use Uber or Uber Eats that often, try to remember to use it earlier in the month, so you don’t forget to use it later on. That’s especially true if you have international travel plans, given that the credit only works in the United States.

    The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in dining credits annually:.

    It has been revealed that what’s my take on the Amex Gold dining credit? Everyone has different spending patterns. Personally, I don’t frequently dine at any of the establishments included with the Amex Gold dining credit, though I do use Grubhub once in a while. So when I can remember to use the perk, that saves me $10 per month on those purchases.

    The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:.

    Let me emphasize that you don’t have to jump through hoops at a restaurant to take advantage of the Amex Gold Resy statement credit. You don’t even have to make your reservation through Resy, as long as it’s a Resy partner restaurant.

    What’s my take on the Amex Gold Resy credit? If you dine out frequently and live in a decently sized city, visiting a Resy restaurant should be super easy. Personally, I’m able to maximize this without even trying, since I go to restaurants associated with Resy all the time.

    It has been revealed that admittedly, this is of limited use to those in small towns, where not many restaurants may use the Resy platform. In those situations, remember to consider Resy restaurants when you’re traveling to a larger city, as that’s your best bet for maximizing that perk.

    The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:.

    You can maximize the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit by spending at least $7 per month at a Dunkin’ location with your eligible card.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s my take on the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit? Admittedly, this is niche, and seems like an odd fit for a premium card. Dunkin’ isn’t exactly a high-end brand, and the $7 credit seems quite random. However, I think this is easy enough to manage. It’s also worth emphasizing that as of now, simply loading your Dunkin’ account through the Dunkin’ app with $7 per month seems to trigger the credit.

    Based on how I read the terms, that’s not even a fluke. The terms say the credit can’t be used for gift cards, though loading a Dunkin’ account isn’t a gift card. So as things right now stand, basically view this as an $84 annual Dunkin’ credit (which you must load monthly, but the credit as such won’t expire).

    Just about any card with perks that are distributed throughout the year and where enrollment is required will have a significant amount of breakage. That’s only natural, and as I see it, it’s a double-edged sword. On the plus side, I view it as an opportunity for savvy consumers to get outsized value from a card. At the same time, “credit card fatigue” is a very real concept.

    According to recent reports, with that in mind, how much do I value the up to $424 in credits offered on the Amex Gold Card? Here’s my general thought process:.

    Recent findings suggest that when all is noted and done, I’d say that I value the credits on the Amex Gold Card as maybe being within $100 of the card’s annual fee, give or take. To me, that essentially puts this Membership Rewards points-earning powerhouse in line with other mid-range cards, in terms of the cost of holding onto it. Everyone’s math will differ, so crunch the numbers to decide how much value the card offers to you.

    The Amex Gold Card is a product you primarily get for the excellent return it offers on everyday spending. The card has a steep annual fee, though the good news is that this can largely be offset thanks to the up to $424 in annual credits it offers. Hopefully, the above is a useful rundown of how each of the Amex Gold Card credits can be used.

    The Amex Gold credits won’t be equally valuable for everyone, but if you dine at Resy restaurants and use Uber (for rides or food delivery) with any frequency, you should be able to recoup much of the annual fee thanks to the credits.

    What do you make of the Amex Gold Card credits, and how much value are you able to get out of them?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific.
    • The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S.
    • French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers unveiled a new interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    Industry observers note that southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    According to recent reports, for French Bee customers, the latest arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    Dear Tunisair: How About A Refund For My Downgrade, Please?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short.
    • At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft.
    • In a recent development, several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

    At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story….

    In a recent development, several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

    Sources indicate that the email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only showed as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

    There was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

    According to recent reports, after the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

    But anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

    It has been revealed that as I mentioned above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

    According to recent reports, we’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

    If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

    Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

    Recent findings suggest that it just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

    Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

    • In a recent development, the Irish flag carrier will install its first-ever Premium Economy cabin, along with all-new lie-flat business class suites and updated economy seats.
    • It has been revealed that the retrofit will come to 10 of the airline's A330 jets, Aer Lingus mentioned in an announcement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aer Lingus announced a major overhaul of its Airbus A330 fleet, modernizing the interior of the aging jets with a complete nose-to-tail retrofit.

    In a recent development, the Irish flag carrier will install its first-ever Premium Economy cabin, along with all-new lie-flat business class suites and updated economy seats. The airline stated it will also continue to offer free Starlink Wi-Fi on the refurbished planes.

    It has been revealed that the retrofit will come to 10 of the airline's A330 jets, Aer Lingus mentioned in an announcement. The airline has a total of 10 A330-300 jets in service, along with two long-range A330-200s, according to Planespotters.net. It was not immediately clear what would happen to the two A330s that are not included in the retrofit.

    Review: Flying Aer Lingus business class across the Atlantic in its current A330 configuration.

    Aer Lingus described the project as one of its "most significant investments in the onboard customer experience in more than a decade.".

    "Our ambition here is simple," Aer Lingus CEO Lynn Embleton said in a statement. "We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort and connectivity, while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.".

    In a recent development, the retrofitted jets will fly transatlantic routes to North America, the airline said, starting on Oct. 1 with flights EI104 and EI105 between Dublin Airport (DUB) and Upcoming York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

    Let's take a closer look at the retrofit.

    Premium economy cabins have become much more widespread among airlines over the past decade, with carriers capitalizing on customers who are willing to pay a premium for more comfort, but are still price-sensitive and won't pay for business class.

    Recent findings suggest that aer Lingus is late to the trend, but clearly ready to commit. The airline will install four rows of premium economy seats in a 2-3-2 configuration for a total of 28 seats.

    The airline chose the Recaro R4 seat, which features a built-in leg-rest and a footrest at each seat, as well as privacy wings at the head to provide a bit of separation between seat-mates. The premium economy seats will have 38 inches of pitch and 8 inches of recline, as well as a width of 18-19 inches.

    Premium economy will also have its own cabin service, with a three-course meal and drinks throughout the flight, along with amenity kits, bedding, and "noise-reducing" headphones to use during the flight.

    The upcoming cabin will be priced squarely in between coach and business class, with fares starting at €700 each way, or about $768.

    The business-class cabin will see a major upgrade, bringing a fresh fresh product to replace one that has become dated.

    Sources indicate that the cabin will feature 28 business-class suites across seven rows in a 1-2-1 layout, giving every passenger direct aisle access. That's two fewer seats than on the current A330-300, but a significant improvement since alternating rows in the existing cabin are configured in a sort of 1-2-2 layout.

    Sources indicate that the Collins Elevation suites feature closing privacy doors — a first for Aer Lingus. Each seat converts to a 78-inch long fully flat bed, and will offer wireless and USB-C charging options.

    Aer Lingus says that it also prepares to revamp its onboard dining experience to showcase "seasonal Irish ingredients and contemporary culinary influences," although the airline did not share specifics. There will also be a self-service bar with drinks and snacks in the cabin.

    The economy cabin will also see new seats with a handful of features aimed at keeping passengers comfortable on long flights, including a six-way adjustable leather headrest.

    Recent findings suggest that every economy seat in the 2-4-2 cabin will have a 4K seat-back screen with Bluetooth connectivity for headphones, plus USB-C charging. A newly introduced in-flight snack station will have bites available after the main meal service.

    The design of economy and the entire plane is recognizably Aer Lingus, with a palette heavy on greens and whites with customized mood lighting to accent the on-board experience.

    According to recent reports, aer Lingus has offered a pleasant business-class product with stellar on-board service and decent availability, but there's no denying that its "hard product" has fallen behind the times. The new refresh will bring the airline up to snuff with competitors, and should elevate the overall product to match the service provided by the excellent cabin crew.

    The fresh premium economy cabin, meanwhile, offers travelers a new way to fly to Ireland and beyond with more space for a more comfortable journey, while helping Aer Lingus capture an increasingly important passenger segment.

    Overall, we're excited to see the upcoming Aer Lingus hit the skies next fall!

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia.
    • Hyatt has confirmed looks for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland.
    • Sources indicate that the hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

    Hyatt has confirmed looks for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

    Sources indicate that the hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

    According to recent reports, there are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

    While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

    Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:.

    “The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”.

    There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

    This will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

    Recent findings suggest that world of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

    First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:.

    It has been revealed that the area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or Latest York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

    I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any….

    The Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

    In a recent development, it’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

    What do you make of prepares for the Park Hyatt Brisbane?

    #19473. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….
    • When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.
    • In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….

    When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

    In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a organization identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”.

    In some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:.

    Industry observers note that while most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order….

    Aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

    In a recent development, british Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

    While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

    Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the firm’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”.

    For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

    PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

    The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

    It has been revealed that for those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

    China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

    Sources indicate that so, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

    It has been revealed that starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

    The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the firm’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

    South African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

    Atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a big operation.

    The callsign is presumably a reflection of the company’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

    Kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

    European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

    In a recent development, airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

    What’s your favorite airline callsign?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024.
    • According to recent reports, former Rep.
    • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    According to recent reports, “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott unveiled his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    Recent findings suggest that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    It has been revealed that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    According to recent reports, he continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against upcoming sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a upcoming life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    Recent findings suggest that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    In a recent development, as he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    In a recent development, then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he noted in a statement at the time.

    Sources indicate that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    In a recent development, “Jim McDermott was as significant as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    The airline intends to use these planes to open up new long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”.

    Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

    We can expect LATAM to offer an all-latest passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline looks to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:.

    Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV demonstrates. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

    Recent findings suggest that LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

    It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

    LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

    It has been revealed that the A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

    LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

    For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

    Industry observers note that while American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

    Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being said, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”.

    While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

    To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

    It has been revealed that in early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline prepares to use to grow into newly introduced markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

    In a recent development, ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is currently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

    LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two newly introduced wide body business class products over the past several years.

    What do you make of LATAM’s newly introduced A321XLR business class?

    #19469. Tech Report: 1 Simple Callout: The Fresh Fix For The Error That Put An American 777 In A Delta 737’s Path

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (758 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: 1 Simple Callout: The Fresh Fix For The Error That Put An American 777 In A Delta 737’s Path

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued latest safety guidance on Thursday, urging airline pilots to verbally identify runways before crossing them, addressing a seemingly minor cockpit oversight that nearly led to a catastrophic collision at John F.
    • Sources indicate that the change follows a January 2023 incident in which an American Airlines Boeing 777-200ER crossed directly into the path of a departing Delta Air Lines 737-900ER.
    • Under FAA Information for Operators 26016, pilots should announce the runway number shown on airport signs before crossing it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued latest safety guidance on Thursday, urging airline pilots to verbally identify runways before crossing them, addressing a seemingly minor cockpit oversight that nearly led to a catastrophic collision at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The recommendation adds a safeguard against pilots inadvertently entering active runways.

    Sources indicate that the change follows a January 2023 incident in which an American Airlines Boeing 777-200ER crossed directly into the path of a departing Delta Air Lines 737-900ER. The Delta pilots rejected takeoff at approximately 105 knots (121 mph; 195 km/h), narrowly avoiding a collision involving aircraft carrying 308 people. Investigators later found that a simple verbal cross-check might have prevented the incident.

    Under FAA Information for Operators 26016, pilots should announce the runway number shown on airport signs before crossing it. The recommendation applies to Part 121 commercial airlines, Part 135 charter operators, and Part 91K fractional operators. It is voluntary guidance, rather than a legally binding requirement, and allows exceptions where equivalent automated aural advisory systems are installed.

    Industry observers note that the procedure is straightforward. A crew cleared to cross Runway 31L should visually check the approaching runway sign and announce its number. If the sign instead identifies Runway 4L, the discrepancy could reveal a navigational error before the aircraft enters an active runway. The FAA believes this additional check could reduce mistakes caused by distractions and multitasking during taxi operations.

    Sources indicate that the recommendation directly addresses findings from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the JFK incident. Investigators concluded that checking runway signs aloud would provide an extra opportunity to detect an incorrect turn, complementing existing procedures requiring crews to visually check for approaching aircraft.

    The FAA explained the value of this additional safeguard.

    "This practice serves as a double-check mechanism, confirming intended actions and preventing misunderstandings regarding clearances.".

    On January 13, 2023, American flight 106, operated by a 777-200 (N754AN), was taxiing at JFK for a flight to London Heathrow Airport (LHR). Meanwhile, Delta flight 1943, operated by a 737-900ER (N914DU), was preparing to depart for Santo Domingo. American's crew had been instructed to cross Runway 31L via Taxiway K, but missed the required turn, continuing toward Runway 4L instead.

    According to recent reports, at approximately 8:44 PM, the American aircraft turned onto Taxiway J as Delta began accelerating down Runway 4L. JFK's Airport Surface Detection Equipment, Model X (ASDE-X), detected the conflict and warned controllers. The local controller immediately canceled Delta's takeoff clearance. The following timeline, reconstructed from the NTSB's investigation, demonstrates how swiftly events unfolded:.

    American misses the turn onto Taxiway K.

    American turns onto Taxiway J; Delta begins takeoff.

    American reaches the runway holding line.

    ASDE-X alerts the control tower.

    Controller cancels Delta's takeoff clearance.

    Delta initiates rejected takeoff.

    Delta reaches approximately 121 mph (195 km/h).

    Delta stops short of the intersection.

    The Delta aircraft eventually stopped approximately 500 feet (152 meters) short of the intersection, having reached its maximum speed just 2,300 feet (700 meters) from where American was crossing. Neither aircraft sustained damage, and all 308 occupants escaped injury. The NTSB concluded that the controller's intervention, prompted by ASDE-X, likely prevented a catastrophic accident reminiscent of the Tenerife Airport Disaster.

    Recent findings suggest that the investigation's most revealing finding was that the American crew had performed their normal crossing checks. According to interviews, the captain declared "cleared to cross" and "clear left," while the first officer responded "clear right." However, neither apparently verified the runway number against airport signage. Investigators found that the signs should have been visible for approximately 10 seconds. The cockpit voice recording had been overwritten, so the precise exchanges could not be independently verified.

    It has been revealed that investigators attributed the error to distractions, multitasking, and a loss of situational awareness. The crew was dealing with delayed weight-and-balance paperwork, while the captain followed a familiar but incorrect taxi route. Runway entrance lights also activated too late to prevent the incursion. Although ASDE-X successfully alerted controllers, the NTSB also called for technology that could warn pilots directly about approaching aircraft and runway conflicts.

    Sources indicate that the JFK near-collision was not an isolated warning about runway safety. Less than a month later, Southwest Airlines and FedEx aircraft narrowly avoided a collision at Austin, demonstrating the importance of multiple safeguards. The FAA's latest recommendation cannot eliminate every runway incursion, but it addresses a particularly preventable mistake: pilots checking that a runway is clear without first confirming it is the correct one.

    Latest Update: Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026.
    • However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee.
    • This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

    However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

    This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

    Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card.

    Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:.

    Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:.

    According to recent reports, with the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited at the moment has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

    Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

    Admittedly the spending requirement is substantial (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

    If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

    Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

    Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

    When it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

    With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

    Sources indicate that in fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

    According to recent reports, no Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history.

    In terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:.

    Recent findings suggest that all cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like that.

    2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

    Meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

    In a recent development, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

    American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

    Sources indicate that this program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

    According to recent reports, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

    In a recent development, you can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

    According to recent reports, personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

    It has been revealed that it’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

    It has been revealed that I think the issue is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back. It’s just not a new concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

    So who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:.

    Sources indicate that I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

    Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

    According to recent reports, perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

    The upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

    In a recent development, another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

    If you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

    Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

    As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

    While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

    The card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

    I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

    I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

    Sources indicate that in addition to a massive welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer. The card also offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

    Sources indicate that ultimately I’d consider this to be a niche card. The card could be worth getting for the excellent welcome offer, and it could be worth it if you have a business that spends a huge amount, and values the lack of a preset spending limit, the card’s Amex branding, and/or the statement credits.

    Industry observers note that beyond that, though, I tend to think there are better options. If you’re not a huge spender, the Amex Blue Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Plus are excellent options. If you’re willing to maximize points and bonus categories, consider the Amex Business Gold. And if you’re looking for the best direct alternative that’s arguably more lucrative, consider the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

    Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
    • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

    The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

    He noted “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

    During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

    Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from upcoming software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

    Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

    It has been revealed that “This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

    The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

    Mullin said the latest $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

    “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

    Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

    Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

    In a recent development, senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

    According to recent reports, the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

    Industry observers note that the committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a upcoming one was built.

    Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

    “Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

    Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

    In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and mentioned their committee would “thoroughly review the problems that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

    Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

    At concern in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa Group prepares to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

    The airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

    Company leaders said their 2024 turnaround proposal, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

    “The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter remarked.

    In a recent development, lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

    Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

    According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

    In a recent development, jetBlue TrueBlue points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you use a JetBlue credit card to pay for your purchase, it wouldn’t code as a JetBlue purchase.

    In a recent development, therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See my guide to the best credit cards for buying points.

    In a recent development, jetBlue TrueBlue has become more interesting on the redemption front in recent years, and there are definitely some ways to get outsized value. For that matter, in some cases people may find value in topping off their points balance, in order to have enough points for a redemption.

    Let’s look at the opportunities to redeem TrueBlue points, first for travel on JetBlue, and then for travel on partner airlines. For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider TrueBlue points to be worth 1.3 cents each.

    When it comes to redeeming on JetBlue, TrueBlue is a revenue based frequent flyer program. That means the cost of an award redemption is correlated to how much a ticket would cost in cash, though it’s not always a consistent cent per point value.

    In my experience, you’ll typically get around 1.3-1.5 cents per TrueBlue point toward the cost of a ticket on JetBlue in economy.

    Just as an example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, which costs $334 if paying cash. If redeeming TrueBlue points, you’d pay 22,500 points plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.46 cents of value per point.

    As another example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to San Francisco, which has both economy and Mint business class. If paying cash, you’d pay $198 or $676. If redeeming points, you’d pay 14,200 points or 47,300 points, plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.35-1.42 cents of value per point.

    It has been revealed that as you can see, these are situations where you probably shouldn’t buy TrueBlue points. For example, there’s no reason to acquire 14,200 points for 1.43 cents each, for a total cost of $203 (plus the $5.60 in taxes & fees), when you could instead just outright buy the ticket for $198.

    One thing to keep in mind is that if you have JetBlue’s most premium card, you can get a 15% award rebate, so maybe there is a little upside there.

    Sources indicate that jetBlue TrueBlue has gotten better about adding redemptions on partner airlines in recent times, including on Qatar Airways, Condor, and United Airlines. We’re also now seeing redemptions added on China Airlines. There’s definitely some value to be had here.

    For example, you could redeem just 47,400 points for Condor business class one-way from Frankfurt to Toronto. That’s an amazing opportunity to buy points and immediately get outsized value.

    As another example, you could redeem 29,600 points for Qatar Airways business class one-way from Munich to Doha. Given the points acquisition costs we’re talking about, that’s an amazing value.

    One caveat I’d just like to add is that partner award availability can be really tough to come by, so only buy points if you have an understanding of what that availability is like.

    It has been revealed that as I see it, the decision of whether to buy points from a particular loyalty program comes down both to how valuable that currency is, and it also comes down to how many ways there are to acquire the currency. So that’s why it’s worth mentioning that JetBlue TrueBlue points are really easy to acquire.

    It has been revealed that at this point, JetBlue partners with virtually all transferable points currencies, so you can earn TrueBlue points through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Wells Fargo, etc. Bilt, Chase, Citi, and Wells Fargo, have 1:1 transfer ratios, while Amex has a 5:4 ratio, and Capital One has a 5:3 ratio.

    It has been revealed that another option is to apply for JetBlue’s co-branded credit cards, which often have large welcome bonuses. Those points of course won’t post anywhere close to instantly, but it’s a good strategy for building up your TrueBlue points balance over time.

    So there’s no shortage of opportunities to earn TrueBlue points — it’s just a function of whether you’d rather part with cash or a points currency.

    Industry observers note that through December 31, 2026, JetBlue is selling TrueBlue points with up to a 125% bonus, an opportunity to buy points for as little as 1.43 cents each. I’d only buy JetBlue points with a specific use in mind. There’s value to be had in some situations, such as if you have a particular Qatar Airways or Condor award you want to book, and there’s availability.
